lesson.title: Explain It to the Duck: Debugging by Talking Out Loud
lesson.summary: Rubber duck debugging means explaining code line by line to an inanimate object or a listener, using the act of explaining itself to surface bugs before anyone responds.
lesson.body:
Sometimes the fastest way to find a bug is not to run the code at all, but to talk about it. Rubber duck debugging means explaining your code out loud, line by line, to a listener who cannot help you, traditionally a literal rubber duck sitting on your desk, though any patient person, or even an empty room, works just as well. The value is not in what the duck says back, since it says nothing. The value is in the act of explaining itself, which often surfaces the bug before you finish the explanation.

This works because explaining code forces a different kind of reading than the one you do while writing it. When you write code, you read it while thinking about what you meant it to do, and it is easy to see what you intended rather than what is actually on the screen. Explaining it out loud, to something that knows nothing about your intentions, forces you to state each line's actual behavior in plain language, one at a time, and that mismatch between what you say and what you meant becomes hard to miss once you have to say it out loud.

Here is a short narrated example. Suppose this function is meant to return the last word of a sentence:

def last_word(sentence):
    words = sentence.split(" ")
    return words[len(words)]

Calling it raises an IndexError. Explaining it to the duck might go like this: "Okay, duck. This function splits the sentence into a list of words, using a space as the separator. Then I want the last word, so I take the item at index equal to the length of the list. Wait. If there are five words, the valid indices are 0 through 4, not 5. len(words) is 5, but there is no words[5]. That's the bug. I need words[len(words) - 1], or just words[-1]." Notice that the duck did not say a word. The bug surfaced the moment the explanation reached the part where the reasoning stopped matching the code.

This connects directly to the general debugging process: rubber duck debugging is really a way of forming and testing a hypothesis, the same as print debugging or using a debugger, except the tool is your own voice instead of a print statement. It costs nothing, requires no setup, and works especially well for logic errors that do not raise an exception, since those are exactly the kind of bug where you are most likely to silently read past your own mistaken assumption unless you are forced to say it out loud.
